title: Local authorities and planners on the draft Heathrow expansion policy
label: 15 September 2026 · Heathrow Expansion NPS evidence
summary: Local council planners and a national planning adviser told the Transport Committee that the draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement (HENPS) has weaknesses: the public consultation felt limited, environmental protections (especially for rivers and local biodiversity) are thin, a new legal label called "critical national growth infrastructure" risks trumping local harms, and the document leaves too much uncertain on roads, housing, noise insulation and who pays. They want clearer accountability, better local funding and stronger safeguards before any decision is taken.

chapters.title: Introductions and the public consultation
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses said the 10-week consultation felt short and patchy; local councils had to step in to engage residents.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome. Please introduce yourselves for the record, starting with Michael.

turns.speaker: Michael Coughlin
turns.text: I'm Michael Coughlin, strategic adviser to the Heathrow Strategic Planning Group, a coalition of local councils around the airport.

turns.speaker: Mark Frost
turns.text: I'm Mark Frost, associate director for the same group. We represent nine local authorities including Hounslow and Ealing; Hounslow is the accountable borough.

turns.speaker: Ian Thynne
turns.text: I'm Ian Thynne, head of environmental planning specialists at the London Borough of Hillingdon, the host authority.

turns.speaker: Anna Sutherland Bamber
turns.text: I'm Anna Sutherland Bamber, representing the National Infrastructure Planning Association—professionals who work on big national planning projects.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The consultation ran for 10 weeks. How accessible and effective was it compared with past national infrastructure consultations?

turns.speaker: Anna Sutherland Bamber
turns.text: It was broadly in line with guidance and similar in form to other national policy consultations.

turns.speaker: Ian Thynne
turns.text: I disagree. For Hillingdon it wasn't good enough. Past rounds had independent observers, lots of local sessions and leaflet drops. This time we weren't sure what the Department did to reach people.

turns.speaker: Michael Coughlin
turns.text: We're between those views: stakeholder engagement felt stronger for organised groups, but public engagement was less extensive, and timing (a summer 10-week window) hurt reach.

chapters.title: Environment and biodiversity concerns
chapters.takeaway: Councils worry HENPS focuses on a few tests and doesn't protect local rivers, habitats and social impacts; they want stronger local controls and accountable environmental governance.

turns.speaker: Dr Arthur
turns.text: Is the HENPS enough to deal with wider environmental issues—like rivers, water and local ecosystems—not just carbon and air quality?

turns.speaker: Ian Thynne
turns.text: No. There's an obsession with the four headline tests and the wider ecological and social impacts get lost. For example, putting rivers under concrete—'culverting'—through the Colne valley isn't properly addressed.

turns.speaker: Mark Frost
turns.text: Biodiversity matters a lot to our councils. There's a national idea called 'biodiversity net gain'—you must improve nature overall—but our worry is it could be met by creating habitats far away, not locally where communities lose green space.

turns.speaker: Dr Arthur
turns.text: But you can't replace a local river with a distant wetland. What if the replacements fail?

turns.speaker: Mark Frost
turns.text: Exactly. The NPS is opaque on enforcement. We want an 'environmentally controlled growth' framework that holds whoever builds this to account, similar to lessons from other airport projects.

turns.speaker: Michael Coughlin
turns.text: We need to measure both quantity and quality of habitat replacement, and to make promoters legally accountable for quality as well as area lost.

turns.speaker: Anna Sutherland Bamber
turns.text: It's an evolving area. Net gain rules are new and promoters, councils and Natural England are still working out how to make them effective. The NPS gives more detail than past statements, but it's a developing field.

turns.speaker: Ian Thynne
turns.text: For Hillingdon, this is a game-changer. The scale of the project should mean more rigorous, locally tailored protections; the NPS currently lacks sufficient 'guardrails'.

chapters.title: The four tests, a possible fifth, and a new legal label
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses accept the headline tests but want either a 'community' test or stronger surface-access accountability; they warned strongly about a new label—'critical national growth infrastructure'—that may trump local harms.

turns.speaker: Alex Mayer
turns.text: Government has four tests—growth, carbon, air quality, noise. Are these the right tests?

turns.speaker: Michael Coughlin
turns.text: Broadly yes, but they aren't complete. Surface access (roads and public transport delivery) might merit being an explicit test with clear accountability.

turns.speaker: Ian Thynne
turns.text: We want a community test. Past expansions left local communities worse off. A community-focused test would force clear, enforceable plans to make locals better off.

turns.speaker: Anna Sutherland Bamber
turns.text: There are actually many more detailed assessments in the NPS. If you keep adding headline tests, you have to ask where you stop. Consistency across sectors matters.

turns.speaker: Steff Aquarone
turns.text: The draft introduces a new phrase—'critical national growth infrastructure' (CNGI). Has that term existed before?

turns.speaker: Anna Sutherland Bamber
turns.text: Not under that exact name. Other sectors use similar ideas—energy has 'critical national priority'—but this exact term looks new here.

turns.speaker: Steff Aquarone
turns.text: Is it normal to invent a new high-weighted planning label inside an NPS?

turns.speaker: Ian Thynne
turns.text: Unusual. The worry is CNGI creates a single big box of 'national benefit' that can't be outweighed by local harms. That tilts the planning balance so local impacts may never lead to refusal.

turns.speaker: Mark Frost
turns.text: The CNGI label, without criteria or rationale, feels subjective. It could make it impossible to 'fail' the project even if serious harms emerge later.

turns.speaker: Anna Sutherland Bamber
turns.text: The examining authority will still review the evidence during the development consent order (DCO) process—a DCO is the detailed, legally binding planning application for large projects—but the label will influence how they weigh things in their recommendation.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So the label may pre-weight the inspector's view before they examine the details?

turns.speaker: Ian Thynne
turns.text: Yes. In normal planning you balance economic, environmental and social impacts equally. This label risks removing that balance.

chapters.title: Surface access, housing and local authority burdens
chapters.takeaway: Councils say the NPS understates impacts on local roads, housing and public services; targets and timings for public transport and construction mitigation are vague, creating risks for residents and councils.

turns.speaker: Jacob Collier
turns.text: The promoters estimate an extra c.60,000 vehicle journeys a day. Does the NPS pay enough attention to local roads?

turns.speaker: Ian Thynne
turns.text: No. The NPS looks at high-level trunk roads but misses local roads. If public transport targets aren't met, all the extra cars hit small residential streets where people live.

turns.speaker: Mark Frost
turns.text: Resilience is key. Daily incidents already clog the network. More vehicles increase delay and wear and tear; local authorities will face extra maintenance costs but the NPS doesn't force promoters to pay for that.

turns.speaker: Jacob Collier
turns.text: Are the public transport mode-share targets achievable?

turns.speaker: Mark Frost
turns.text: Targets could be achievable if you spend enough on rail and bus, but the NPS leaves uncertain the timing: if rail comes late, roads will suffer in the meantime.

turns.speaker: Ian Thynne
turns.text: And remember we must also deliver tens of thousands of new homes in the borough—those needs use the same roads and services, so everything is squeezed.

turns.speaker: Ashley Dalton
turns.text: On local services—schools, healthcare, housing—does the NPS address the extra demand on councils?

turns.speaker: Michael Coughlin
turns.text: No. It underestimates cumulative impacts. There's pressure on housing from workers and displaced residents, and councils need clear funding to manage that.

turns.speaker: Ashley Dalton
turns.text: What about compensation and compulsory purchase—the 2018 approach is being retained. Is that sufficient?

turns.speaker: Ian Thynne
turns.text: We face the loss of hundreds of properties and unclear eligibility for a wider property offer zone. That uncertainty wrecks local planning: how many school places? Which community buildings are lost and who pays to replace them?

turns.speaker: Mark Frost
turns.text: Compensation wording is confused: property buy-outs, noise insulation, and a '£50m-a-year' community fund are all mentioned but not clearly linked or updated for inflation. Governance is missing.

turns.speaker: Michael Coughlin
turns.text: Councils want mechanisms to capture some airport growth benefits—business rates or bespoke funds—to invest locally in skills, housing and services. The NPS mentions this but it's not strong enough.

chapters.title: Noise mitigation, delivery and legal risk
chapters.takeaway: Current noise insulation schemes helped, but roll-out is slow and under-resourced; the NPS leaves too much conditional language, and they expect legal challenges which would delay things.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How effective have existing noise schemes been, and will they cope with expansion?

turns.speaker: Ian Thynne
turns.text: They've helped but delivery is slow and not properly regulated. The scheme is delivered mainly by the airport on its terms, so prioritisation can be unclear.

turns.speaker: Mark Frost
turns.text: Take-up has improved because Heathrow now funds 100% of some insulation, but regulator decisions cut back planned spend. Heathrow once proposed insulating homes faster; under current funding it could take 100+ years to reach everyone.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: There's a funding gap compared with Gatwick: Gatwick offers about £6,500 per property, Heathrow £3,000. Does that look right?

turns.speaker: Ian Thynne
turns.text: The £3,000 figure isn't properly justified in the draft policy. It barely buys anything and isn't indexed for inflation. Noise annoyance thresholds have changed but mitigation triggers haven't.

turns.speaker: Mark Frost
turns.text: Plus new noise exposure will mean higher construction costs for new homes and community buildings. The NPS doesn't fully factor in those extra costs for local authorities.

turns.speaker: Anna Sutherland Bamber
turns.text: On legal process: big national projects often face judicial review (a court challenge) after a decision. The NPS has tried to respond to past legal points, but more challenge is likely and that adds time and uncertainty.

turns.speaker: Michael Coughlin
turns.text: The draft mixes a vision with vague delivery language—lots of 'may', 'should', 'seek to'—which makes it weak on what will actually be enforced. Councils need clear, accountable commitments.

turns.speaker: Alex Mayer
turns.text: So, to close: is the draft NPS fit to be policy as it stands?

turns.speaker: Ian Thynne
turns.text: Not as it stands. It risks guaranteeing consent by using the CNGI label and leaves communities exposed. If it must proceed, councils need stronger, enforceable protections and proper funding up front.

turns.speaker: Mark Frost
turns.text: And there must be assurance that affordability arguments won't be used later to remove critical mitigation. If mitigation is carved away for cost, communities will bear the harms.

turns.speaker: Anna Sutherland Bamber
turns.text: Policy inconsistency across sectors is also an issue. The NPS has improved on some points but will still be scrutinised in courts and needs clearer definitions and delivery rules.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. If there's more you couldn't fit in today, please write in. The Committee will take these concerns—especially about CNGI, local funding and environmental safeguards—into account.

glossary.definition: A coalition of local councils around Heathrow airport working together on planning and strategy.
A professional body for people who work on large, national infrastructure planning projects in the UK.
The local council formally responsible for coordinating and answering for a project in its area.
The local council in whose area a major project (like an airport) is physically located and which leads local planning duties.
Likely short for the Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement, the specific policy document for Heathrow expansion.
Placing a stream or river into a covered channel or pipe, usually underground or under concrete.
A rule requiring development to leave nature in a better state overall than before construction.
The UK government body responsible for protecting and improving England’s natural environment.
National Policy Statement: a government policy document setting rules and objectives for major national infrastructure projects.
A label the draft policy uses to mark projects claimed to be vital for national growth, giving them high planning weight.
Abbreviation for 'critical national growth infrastructure', used to denote projects given strong national-benefit priority.
The formal body or inspector that reviews evidence and makes recommendations on major infrastructure planning applications.
The organisations or developers proposing and driving a major infrastructure project.
A defined area where special compensation or purchase schemes may be offered to affected property owners.
A legal power allowing public bodies to force the sale of private land or property for public projects, with compensation.
Goals specifying what share of trips should be made by public transport rather than private cars.
Major highways and main roads managed nationally or regionally, carrying long-distance traffic.
A proposed annual fund of £50 million intended to support communities affected by the project.
Set levels of noise exposure at which authorities trigger mitigation measures for affected homes and people.
A proposed planning requirement to show a project will deliver clear, enforceable benefits to local communities.
